schools.summary: Gregory the Great reads the renewed assault as proof of Job's growth — the enemy, defeated, only multiplied his excellences, and 'Whence comest thou?' cannot be asked as before, for Satan returns beaten from the contest.

Henry sets a court reconvened: the sworn enemy renews his malicious prosecution, coming not to confess but with a further design, the accuser of the brethren who charges them day and night (Rev. 12:10).
Gill takes the 'sons of God' as worshippers and reckons the interval short — days or a fortnight — rejecting the Targum's year, since Satan would grant no breathing-time nor the friends wait so long.

Clarke thinks the interval probably a whole year (the Targum's annual atonement), and reads the scene metaphorically: Satan can hurt none but by God's permission, granted only to be overruled for God's glory and the sufferer's good.
Ellicott ties 'Satan came also' to Job 1:7 and notes Peter's verb for the adversary, whence 'peripatetic,' the walker to and fro.

debates.question: How long was the interval between the first and second councils?

sides.position: a short space — days, a week, or a fortnight at most
about a whole year, at the season of the annual atonement

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch note the purpose-clause now repeated of Satan himself, come with a definite object, and the slight variation in the word for 'whence' from Job 1:7 — a common feature of Scripture's repetitions, not a change of sense.
Gill marks that the same question is put and the same restless answer returned, Satan presenting himself again among the sons of God as though nothing had passed.
Keil and Delitzsch draw the conclusion that there was no prior reason for the injury, and gloss 'movedst' (against Umbreit) not as 'lead astray' but as instigate/incite to evil (cf. 1 Chron. 21:1).

Wesley: 'movedst,' like the rest, is not literal but signifies the devil's malice and God's permission for wise ends; Clarke weighs 'destroy without cause' and traces the verb (swallow/devour) to Peter's roaring lion (1 Pet. 5:8).
Gill notes the commendation enlarged: Job a gainer, not a loser, in character by his trials.

Clarke reads 'skin for skin' as a man parting with all, limb by limb, to save his life (the Targum's sense, hence 'save his life'); Wesley presses Satan's charge that Job's patience is not piety but self-love and policy.

Ellicott makes it a sharper form of the insinuation of Job 1:9 — Job's quid pro quo; Keil and Delitzsch survey and reject the rival construals of Olshausen, Hupfeld, and Hirzig/Ewald, holding to the plain self-preservation sense.
Gill hears Satan still refusing to own Job, insinuating a selfish, mercenary service that keeps its religion only while health and ease remain.

themes: the terms of the second trial

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch read the coming permission: Job's life is to be placed in extreme peril but not forfeited, to test whether he will deny God in the face of death; the word is the soul that produces the spirit-life, though rendered 'life.'
Gill takes the demand as the motion for a second trial — God to withdraw the hand of providence over Job's health and fill his flesh and bones with disease and rottenness.
Clarke exposes the veiled curse: 'curse thee to thy face' is literally 'if he will not bless thee,' a euphemism; Satan wagers that Job's piety is only regulated by God's bounty.

themes: touch his bone and his flesh

schools.summary: Clarke marvels at the economy of salvation — the destroyer made, by God's order, the preserver of Job's life; Wesley reads the limit as mercy (God chains the roaring lion) and Job as a type of Christ, whose heel and life Satan was suffered to touch.
Gill wonders that a saint is given into Satan's hand, but denies Job is thereby off God's heart or the devil's property: nothing can separate him from the love of God.
Ellicott: God's faithfulness cannot fail though Job's should (2 Tim. 2:13); One cared for Job's life more than he did himself.

Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott identify the disease as elephantiasis, the most fearful leprosy (limbs like an elephant's, skin clotted and cracked), echoing the curse of Deut. 28:35; Keil notes it struck even Baldwin of Jerusalem.
Henry sees Satan turn from persecutor to tormentor, smiting Job head to foot with boils as if set on fire of hell, and warns how far Satan may have a hand in disease (Luke 13:16).

Clarke queries whether it was smallpox rather than leprosy (the itching, the separate pustules, the fever); Wesley keeps the biblical echo of the boils of Egypt, threatened against apostate Israel (Deut. 28:27).
Gill notes only that Satan, having his leave, departed at once, eager to execute his malice.

debates.question: What was the nature of Job's disease?

sides.position: elephantiasis, the most extreme form of leprosy
possibly the smallpox rather than leprosy, given the itching and separate pustules

schools.summary: Gill hears the silence first — no murmuring or cursing — as Job takes a broken pot to scrape away the matter of his boils, left untended by servants and wife who stand off from the stench.
Henry dwells on the destitution: no salves, only a shard that rakes the wounds; none to tend him, for men are lovers of their own selves, unthankful, without natural affection.
Wesley reads the potsherd and ashes as tokens of deep humiliation, Job declining all tenderness and sitting content where God has laid him.
Keil and Delitzsch note plainly that he sat down among the ashes.

Keil and Delitzsch take 'renounce God, and die' as 'take leave of God' — Satan's own aim — yet with Hengstenberg allow her desperation may spring from love; Ellicott feels the pain of a foe within one's household (Micah 7:6; Matt. 10:36).
Clarke reads the verb as 'bless,' a savage irony ('Bless God, and die!'), noting the LXX's expanded lament; Wesley hears the same sarcasm — bless God for thy losses, and die as a fool dieth.
Henry reads her as Satan's spared instrument, sent to tempt as Eve tempted Adam, bantering Job's integrity and urging the blackest counsels of blasphemy and self-murder.
Gill inclines to think her a good woman, in the dark under a sore temptation, and doubts the Targum's identification of her with Dinah.

debates.question: Did Job's wife speak as Satan's malicious instrument or out of grief and love?

sides.position: Satan's spared instrument, sent to tempt him to blasphemy and self-murder
a good woman under sore temptation, her desperation born of love
holders: Hengstenberg (as reported by Keil and Delitzsch)

debates.question: What does 'curse God, and die' mean?

sides.position: an open imprecation — curse God and be done
a bitter irony, the verb really 'bless' — 'Bless God, and die!'
'take leave of God,' as Job's answer shows

themes: curse or bless God, and die
the surest hand for the poison

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch sharpen the rebuke — not 'foolish women' but 'one of the ungodly,' one who thinks madly and acts impiously, softened by 'one of'; Ellicott finds Job's words wiser than he knew, receiving evil transmuting calamity to blessing, in contrast with Christ's temptation (Matt. 26:39; Heb. 5:8).
Henry reads a temptation resisted ('Get thee behind me, Satan'): good and evil come not from contrary causes but both from God's hand, and to receive evil is to take it as a gift.

Clarke: God's blessings were only lent, so why be offended when the Owner reclaims them? Wesley: shall worms give laws to their Lord, when past mercies outweigh short corrections and the affliction may make us partakers of his holiness? Let murmuring be excluded.
Gill: Job says she speaks 'as one of' the foolish, not that she is one — a good woman speaking out of character.

outliers.note: Marks the Chaldee's qualification of 'did not sin with his lips' — that Job sinned not in speech, yet 'in his heart he thought words' — a reservation the other witnesses do not press.

themes: as one of the foolish/ungodly women
shall we receive good and not evil
did not sin with his lips

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch mark the seventh temptation as the real conflict's start and place the friends (Teman famed for wisdom, Jer. 49:7); Ellicott notes Eliphaz's Esau-descent may date the book and that Zophar's district is unknown.

Clarke traces the genealogy and locates Job in Edom, his friends in Arabia Petraea, their wisdom proven by their speeches; Wesley finds the piety preserved among these non-covenant men a happy presage of grace to the Gentiles.
Henry turns to their friendship — a brother born for adversity — who came unbidden by appointment to mourn and comfort, yet through unskilful handling proved miserable comforters.
Gill notes the three friends, men of correspondence with Job, coming to pay a friendly visit under his calamity.

themes: an appointment to mourn and comfort

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch describe a form that seemed Job but could not be recognized, the dust flung toward heaven being the sign of a suffering that cries to heaven; Ellicott contrasts 'knew him not' with the father who knew his lost son afar off (Luke 15:20).
Clarke sets the rent garments and strewn dust among the universal signs of profound grief used by all nations.
Gill pictures the moment of recognition failing, whether at a distance or on entering the room.

Keil and Delitzsch deny custom prescribed the silence (against Ewald): it was the force of the impression and fear of annoying Job, betraying that they had not grasped their purpose — a pity they let him speak first; Ellicott admires the colossal grandeur and hoary antiquity of the poem.

Clarke gathers the seven-day mourning parallels (Jacob, Saul, Ezekiel) — they treated Job as dead — and with Wesley judges their silence sprang partly from a suspicion that he suffered for secret crimes; Wesley also names their grief and astonishment.
Gill explains the seven days and nights as the usual mourning term, the friends sitting the greater part of each, conforming to Job in sympathy.

debates.question: Why did the friends sit silent seven days?

sides.position: the sheer force of his grief and their dismay and astonishment
a suspicion that he suffered for some secret crime, so they knew not what to say
custom and propriety prescribed the seven days' silence
holders: Ewald (as reported by Keil and Delitzsch)
